examDifficulty.heading: Is the Consumer Goods Cloud TPM Accredited Professional Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: It is a moderate exam, but it needs business knowledge as well as Salesforce skills. You have to understand how trade promotions work in the consumer goods industry: funds, tactics, baselines, lift and claims.
bullets: About 66% to pass, roughly 39 correct answers. Check the official guide for the current figure.
Business terms. Baseline volume, incremental volume, trade spend, ROI and deductions all come up.
The full cycle. Plan, fund, run, settle and review promotions.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: People who have worked on promotion planning for a consumer goods brand do best. Before you book. Aim for 80% or more on practice tests and be able to explain how a promotion's ROI is worked out.

examFormat.heading: Consumer Goods Cloud TPM Accredited Professional Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: Accredited Professional exams are taken online. Here is what to expect:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Most questions describe a step in the promotion cycle, such as setting a budget, planning a price cut or paying a retailer's claim, and ask how the system handles it.
bestWayToPass: Follow one promotion end to end: Account plan, promotion, tactics, funding, execution, claims and post-event review.
Learn the money side: Funds, budgets, accruals, payments and how claims are matched to promotions.
Understand baselines: Baseline volume is what would sell anyway. Incremental volume is the extra the promotion drives.
Know where data comes from: Shipments from the ERP and sell-out from retailer data.

certificationCard.description: This exam tests how you set up and use Consumer Goods Cloud Trade Promotion Management: account planning, promotions and tactics, funds, claims and settlement, and promotion analytics.

keyConcepts.h2: Consumer Goods TPM AP: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Trade Promotion Planning & Fund Management
blocks.body: Consumer goods companies pay retailers to promote their products, and this **trade spend** is often one of their biggest costs. Planning starts with an **account plan** for each retailer, showing targets for volume, revenue and spend. Money comes from **funds**, which hold budgets for a period, a customer or a product group. Some funds are fixed amounts. Others grow with sales, for example a few cents per case shipped. Promotions draw on these funds, so the system can show how much is planned, committed and spent.

blocks.heading: Promotion Execution & Tactics
blocks.body: A **promotion** covers a time period, a retailer and a set of products. Inside it, **tactics** describe what will happen, such as a temporary price reduction, an in-store display or a feature in the retailer's flyer. Each tactic has a cost and an expected effect on sales. Promotions move through statuses like planning, approved and completed, and approval rules can check that spend stays within the fund. Templates help teams create common promotion types quickly and consistently.

blocks.heading: Settlement & Claims Processing
blocks.body: After a promotion, the retailer asks to be paid, either by sending a **claim** or by taking a **deduction** off the next invoice. Settlement means matching that claim or deduction to the right promotion and tactic, checking the amount, and approving the **payment**. If the claim is higher than what was agreed, the difference needs to be checked before paying. Good settlement keeps trade spend accurate and stops paying twice for the same activity.

blocks.heading: Forecasting & Baseline Analytics
blocks.body: **Baseline volume** is what would have sold without the promotion. **Incremental volume** is the extra volume the promotion drives. The promotion's value is worked out from the incremental profit compared with its cost, giving its **ROI**. Planners use history to forecast how a new promotion will perform, and **post-event analysis** compares the forecast with what really happened. Over time, this shows which tactics and retailers give the best return.

blocks.heading: Integration with ERP & Retailer Data
blocks.body: TPM depends on good data. **Shipments** (sell-in) and invoices usually come from the ERP. **Point-of-sale** data (sell-out) comes from retailers or data providers. Product and account hierarchies are loaded so promotions can be planned at the right level, such as a brand or a retailer group. Payments and deductions often flow back to the ERP for finance. Keeping product and customer IDs consistent across systems is key to matching all this data.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce Consumer Goods Trade Promotion Management Accredited Professional Exam
scenarioTips.intro: Most questions place you at one step of the promotion cycle. Work out which record or number matters at that step.

blocks.heading: Trade Promotion Planning
blocks.body: Plans start at the account level, with targets for volume, revenue and spend. Promotions and tactics sit under them.

blocks.heading: Fund Management
blocks.body: Funds hold budgets. Fixed funds have a set amount. Variable funds grow with sales. Promotions draw down funds.

blocks.heading: Account Planning
blocks.body: Account plans compare targets with planned promotions, so key account managers can see gaps early.

blocks.heading: Promotion Settlement & Claims
blocks.body: Match each claim or deduction to the right promotion and tactic before paying. Check differences first.

blocks.heading: Analytics for TPM
blocks.body: ROI depends on incremental volume, not total volume. Compare forecast with actual after every promotion.

sampleQuestions.question: A promotion sold 12,000 cases. Without it, the product would have sold about 9,000 cases. What is the incremental volume?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Incremental volume is the extra volume caused by the promotion: total minus baseline, so 12,000 minus 9,000.
whyWrong: 12,000 is total volume, which includes sales that would have happened anyway.
Adding them together has no meaning here.
9,000 is the baseline.

sampleQuestions.question: A brand gives each retailer 5 cents for every case shipped, to be spent on promotions. What kind of fund is this?
options: A variable fund that grows with shipments
A fixed fund holding a set amount of money
sampleQuestions.explanation: The amount depends on how many cases are shipped, so the fund grows with volume.
whyWrong: A deduction is money the retailer takes off an invoice.
A fixed fund has a set amount decided in advance.
A claim is a retailer's request to be paid.

sampleQuestions.question: A retailer runs a temporary price cut and an in-store display during the same two-week promotion. How should these be recorded?
options: As two entirely separate account plans
As two tactics within one promotion
sampleQuestions.explanation: Tactics describe the activities within a promotion, each with its own cost and effect.
whyWrong: Account plans cover the whole year for a retailer.
Funds pay for tactics, they don't describe them.
Claims come after the promotion.

sampleQuestions.question: After a promotion, a retailer takes $8,000 off their next invoice. What is this called?
options: A deduction matched to the promotion
sampleQuestions.explanation: Deductions are amounts the retailer takes off an invoice, which must be matched and checked against what was agreed.
whyWrong: A tactic is a planned activity.
Baseline is a volume measure.
A fund is a budget.

sampleQuestions.question: A claim is $2,000 higher than the agreed tactic cost. What should happen?
options: Raise the budget on the fund automatically each time
Investigate the difference before approving payment
Pay the full claim straight away
sampleQuestions.explanation: Differences should be checked before paying, so the company doesn't overpay.
whyWrong: Raising the budget hides the problem.
Deleting the promotion loses the record.
Paying without checking risks paying for things that weren't agreed.

sampleQuestions.question: Which number best shows whether a promotion was worth the money?
options: ROI from incremental profit against cost
The overall length of the promotion
sampleQuestions.explanation: ROI looks at the extra profit the promotion created against what it cost.
whyWrong: Total volume includes sales that would have happened anyway.
More tactics doesn't mean better results.
Length doesn't measure value.

sampleQuestions.question: Where does shipment (sell-in) data usually come from?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Shipments and invoices are recorded in the ERP and loaded into TPM.
whyWrong: Funds hold budgets.
Account plans hold targets.
The flyer is a promotion activity.

sampleQuestions.question: Planners want to see how a promotion actually performed against its forecast. What should they run?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Post-event analysis compares forecast with actual results, which improves future planning.
whyWrong: A fund transfer moves budget.
A claim is a payment request.
An account plan sets targets for the future.

sampleQuestions.question: A key account manager wants to check whether planned promotions will meet the year's volume target for a retailer. Where should they look?
options: The invoice list held in the ERP
sampleQuestions.explanation: Account plans compare targets with planned promotions, showing gaps early.
whyWrong: Price alone doesn't show targets.
One claim shows one payment.
Invoices show past sales, not plans against targets.

sampleQuestions.question: A promotion's planned spend would go over what is left in its fund. What should the process do?
options: Flag it through approval rules beforehand
Approve the claim automatically without review
sampleQuestions.explanation: Approval rules can check spend against available funds before a promotion goes ahead.
whyWrong: Ignoring funds defeats budget control.
Deleting the fund loses budget tracking.
Automatic approval risks overspending.

sampleQuestions.question: Retailer point-of-sale data arrives weekly from a data provider. Why is it useful in TPM?
options: It shows what consumers actually bought
It sets the budgets held on each fund
sampleQuestions.explanation: Sell-out data shows real consumer purchases, which helps measure promotion effect.
whyWrong: Tactics are planned by users.
The ERP still holds shipments and invoices.
Budgets are set separately.

sampleQuestions.question: Promotions should be planned at the brand level for a retailer group, not item by item. What must be in place?
options: A separate new fund for each of the items
sampleQuestions.explanation: Hierarchies let users plan at higher levels, like brand and retailer group, and roll numbers up and down.
whyWrong: A separate org isn't needed.
Spreadsheets bypass the system.
A fund per item is the opposite of planning at brand level.

sampleQuestions.question: Teams keep setting up the same kind of promotion from scratch. What would save time and keep them consistent?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Templates pre-fill common promotion types, so they are faster to create and set up the same way.
whyWrong: Length doesn't affect setup time.
Fewer tactics may not match the plan.
More funds don't speed up setup.

sampleQuestions.question: Why must product and customer IDs match across TPM, the ERP and retailer data?
options: So shipments, sell-out and claims can be matched
So that the company's website loads a little faster
sampleQuestions.explanation: Consistent IDs let the system tie each piece of data to the right product, customer and promotion.
whyWrong: Costs are set by the tactic, not the ID.
Matching IDs doesn't add money to funds.
Website speed is unrelated.

sampleQuestions.question: A promotion lifted volume a lot, but the price cut was so deep that profit fell. What does this show?
options: Every promotion that shows a sales lift is also profitable
High volume lift doesn't always mean a good ROI
sampleQuestions.explanation: ROI depends on profit, not just volume. A deep discount can drive volume while losing money.
whyWrong: Lift and profit are not the same thing.
Baselines are needed to measure lift.
Fund size doesn't explain lost profit.
